why-output-formatting.title: Avionics Dashboard Engineering
why-output-formatting.content:
### The Chaos of Unformatted Streams

When Scout Drone Sigma transmits high-frequency telemetry back to Mission Control on Earth, human flight directors must evaluate critical systems at a glance.

Consider raw default `cout` output:
```text
SENSOR READING THRESH
BATTERY 12.3456 14
CORE_TEMP 78.9 80
RADAR 108.2001 120
```
Because numbers have different digit lengths, columns zigzag across the screen, decimal points drift wildly, and parsing data becomes hazardous during flight maneuvers.

To produce clear, professional telemetry displays, C++ provides the **`<iomanip>`** (Input/Output Manipulators) header.

With `<iomanip>`, you can:
- Enforce strict column widths using `setw(width)`.
- Align text cleanly to the `left` or `right`.
- Fix decimal precision with `fixed` and `setprecision(digits)`.
- Guarantee that every flight report matches Mission Control specifications down to the exact character.

iomanip-architecture.title: Stream Manipulator Architecture
iomanip-architecture.content:
### Inside the Output Stream Formatter

Manipulators modify the internal state of the `cout` output stream.

![C++ iomanip Architecture](assets/l26-iomanip-anatomy.en.svg)

#### The Golden Rules of Formatting

1. **Width is Single-Shot:**
   - `setw(n)` sets the field width **only for the immediate next variable printed**!
   - Immediately after outputting that variable, the stream automatically resets its field width back to `0` (default).
   - *Example:* `cout << setw(5) << 42 << 100;` prints `"   42100"`.

2. **Precision and Alignment are Sticky:**
   - `fixed`, `setprecision(p)`, `left`, and `right` are persistent ("sticky"). Once set, they remain active for all subsequent outputs until explicitly changed.

3. **The `fixed` Requirement:**
   - Without `fixed`, `setprecision(n)` controls total *significant digits* (for example, `12.345` with precision 2 becomes `12`).
   - With `fixed`, `setprecision(n)` controls exact digits *after the decimal point* (`12.35`). Always combine: `cout << fixed << setprecision(2);`.

write-aligned-column-table.title: Flight Manifest: Two-Column Table
write-aligned-column-table.content:
### Building an Aligned Flight Roster

Write a program to format a manifest of drone subsystem status codes.

Input:
1. An integer `n`.
2. `n` lines, each containing a subsystem name (string) and an integer status code.

For each subsystem, print a single line with:
- Subsystem name left-aligned with width 10 (`left << setw(10) << name`).
- Status code right-aligned with width 6 (`right << setw(6) << code`).
write-aligned-column-table.task:
1. Read integer `n` from `cin`.
2. Loop `n` times reading string `name` and integer `code`.
3. Format each row using `left << setw(10) << name << right << setw(6) << code`.
4. Output each formatted row followed by a newline.

capstone-flight-telemetry-dashboard.title: Autonomous Avionics Telemetry Dashboard
capstone-flight-telemetry-dashboard.content:
### Mission Control Flight Report Generator

Implement Sigma's complete avionics reporting module.

Input:
1. Integer `n` (number of telemetry channels).
2. `n` lines, each containing `string name`, `double reading`, and `double threshold`.

Requirements:
1. Print the table header line:
   `left << setw(10) << "SENSOR" << right << setw(10) << "READING" << setw(9) << "THRESH"`
2. For each channel, print:
   `left << setw(10) << name << right << fixed << setprecision(2) << setw(10) << reading << setw(9) << threshold`
3. Calculate the average of all `reading` values across all `n` channels.
4. Print `AVERAGE: <avg>` formatted with `fixed` and `setprecision(2)`.
capstone-flight-telemetry-dashboard.task:
1. Read integer `n` from `cin`.
2. Print the formatted header line with widths 10, 10, and 9.
3. Loop `n` times reading `name`, `reading`, and `threshold`.
4. Print each row using `left` for name and `right` with `fixed << setprecision(2)` for the numeric columns.
5. Compute the arithmetic mean of all readings.
6. Print `AVERAGE: <avg>` formatted to 2 decimal places.

recap.title: Summary: I/O Formatting Mastery
recap.content:
### Chapter 26 Complete: Precision Formatting

Scout Drone Sigma's flight reports are now aligned to perfection, ready for real-time mission telemetry ingestion.

#### Manipulator Quick Reference

| Manipulator | Type | Behavior |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `setw(n)` | Single-Shot | Sets field width for the **immediate next** variable only |
| `left` | Sticky | Aligns text to the left margin of the field |
| `right` | Sticky | Aligns text to the right margin of the field (default) |
| `fixed` | Sticky | Formats floating points in standard decimal notation |
| `setprecision(n)` | Sticky | With `fixed`, controls exact count of digits after `.` |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Because `setw()` is single-shot, you must repeat `setw(w)` before **every single column** you output in a table loop!

Next in Chapter 27: **Structures (`struct`)** — bundling related flight parameters (coordinates, battery, velocity) into unified custom data types.
